label: Random seed
tooltip: The Random seed is a number used to reproduce model results. If you rerun the model with the same settings, inputs, and random seed value, you will obtain identical results.

label: Probabilistic sensitivity iterations
tooltip:
This model includes a Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA), which runs multiple simultaneous iterations.

Each iteration randomly draws parameters based on means and standard errors reported in the literature to produce a unique result. Together, the iterations can show the degree of uncertainty around the model's base case result.

Warning: Large values (>10,000) may slow down the model significantly, depending on the Time horizon.

To find out more about the PSA, click the ? button.

label: Time horizon (years)
tooltip:
How long are simulated patients tracked?

Warning: Long time horizons (>10 years) can slow down the model run time, depending on the number of PSA iterations.

label: Artificial standard errors (% of the mean)
tooltip:
This value applies to input parameters with unknown standard errors and confidence intervals. An assumed standard error equal to 20% of the parameter mean is the industry standard "rule of thumb" used in health economic modelling.

Changing this value can produce scenario analyses in which we are more or less confident about the accuracy of reported input parameters in the model.

Example: If we obtained ambulance costs from a single emergency department, we would increase this value. If we sourced ambulance from a reliable government database, we could decrease this value.

label: Country & currency
tooltip: Select the country from which the health resource cost data are sourced.

label: Willingness-to-pay (WTPg>) default threshold
tooltip:
How much is a health system willing to pay for an improvement equivalent to adding 1 year of full and healthy life? This value represents a decision rule for treatments that are better but more expensive than the current standard care.

Some Health Technology Assessment (HTA) agencies will produce explicit country-specific values. For example, the UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence considers treatments below £20,000 per Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gained to be cost-effective and therefore "good value for money".

Click the WTP link to find out more.

label: WTP range
tooltip: Some countries have a range of cost-effectiveness thresholds. For example, the UK will mostly accept treatments estimated at £20,000 per Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gained, and reject treatments that add 1 QALY to the health system for more than £30,000. Within the £20-30K range, the reimbursement decision is uncertain.

label: Number of patients
tooltip:
How many patients should the model simulate? Use the settings below to customise the simulated patient cohort.

Higher numbers (>1,000) will improve the model's accuracy, but may slow down the run time, depending on the time horizon and PSA iterations.

label: Patient starting age range
tooltip: Each patient's age at the start of the simulation will be randomly sampled from a uniform distribution and will impact their simulated time-to-death.

label: Included cancers
tooltip: Which cancer populations should the simulated patients be sampled from? You must select at least 1 cancer type.

label: Included patients with _ years of prior cancer survival
tooltip: How many years have the simulated patients survived with a cancer diagnosis before the start of ePROM monitoring (i.e., before entering the model)? This impacts their simulated time-to-death. The model will randomly sample patient characteristics from the options you select (you must select at least 1).

label: Scenario assumptions of ePROM benefits
choiceNames: Survival benefit , Fewer ED visits , Fewer ambulance trips , Improved quality of life
tooltip:
Scenario Analyses

The model will produce different results depending on the assumptions selected. For each assumption, you may click on the links to review the published literature from which it was sourced, and decide whether it is appropriate for the ePROM intervention you wish to simulate.

For example, Denis and Lizée report that ePROM monitoring leads to a survival benefit and reduction in ambulance trips. However, this evidence comes from a clinical trial in lung cancer patients, which may not apply to other cancer groups or intervention designs. Furthermore, the death hazard ratio may overestimate survival of ePROM-monitored patients beyond the trial's time horizon.

label: Scenario assumption: effect of patient adherence on ePROM reporting
choiceNames:
No effect
Higher adherence does not increase alerts., Random
Higher adherence increases alerts proportionally., Mixed / uncertain
Higher adherence somewhat increases alerts.
tooltip:
The paper by Girgis et al. (2020) reports that 328 patients in the intervention arm of the trial completed 2,746 assessments via PROMPT-Care (an ePROM intervention) and generated 877 email alerts sent to clinicians over the course of the trial period. These values are used to calculate symptom rates in this model.

However, the paper also reports a patient adherence rate of 67% (i.e., 23% of patients did not complete ePROM assessments as intended).

If patient adherence was higher, would they have generated more alerts?
Is the missingness random, or can we assume that non-adherent patients simply had no symptoms to report?

The model will produce slightly different results depending on the assumption chosen.

label:
ePROM missingness assumption
What percentage of missed ePROM assessments are random?
tooltip:
Enter the share of missing ePROM data that could have resulted in severe symptom alerts under higher patient adherence. A higher value (>50%) strengthens the effect of adherence in the model.

If you enter a lower value (<50%), you assume that most missing ePROM data is explained by patients who are healthy and have no symptoms to report, which weakens the effect of adherence in the model.

label: Patient adherence & healthcare professional (HCP) engagement
choiceNames:
Use default parameters
Patient adherence = 67%
Alerts reviewed by HCP = 44%
, Input custom parameters
tooltip:
For patients to benefit from ePROM monitoring, we assume that two conditions need to be met:

1. The patient reports symptoms via ePROMs.
2. The healthcare professional (HCP) reviews the symptom report or alert and takes action.

By default, this model uses results from Girgis et al. (2020) to calculate symptom rates (based on alerts), patient adherence, and HCP engagement.

If you wish to test the impact of different levels of adherence and engagement, select Input custom parameters.

label:
Patient adherence
Probability that a patient self-reports ePROMs when required or after experiencing symptoms.
tooltip:
Whenever a patient experiences serious symptoms that would benefit from ePROM monitoring and a HCP response, what is the probability that the patient reports those symptoms via ePROMs?

Example: If this value is 50%, then patients will only report half of the symptoms they experience. The other half of the symptoms will remain unreported and therefore will not be addressed through ePROM monitoring.

label:
HCP engagement
Share of ePROM reports/alerts reviewed by HCPs.
tooltip:
Whenever a healthcare professional (HCP) receives a ePROM report or symptom alert, what is the probability that they will be able to review and address it?

Example: If this value is 50%, then HCPs will only review half of the ePROM reports or symptom alerts. The other half of the symptoms will not be processed through ePROM monitoring and can only be addressed through usual care (e.g., in-person appointments).

How much does it cost to monitor ePROMs per 1 patient each month?

This may include time spent by staff, software costs, etc. This
does not include upfront costs, such as research, implementation, training, etc.

There is a wide variation of cost estimates reported in the literature. This model tests a range of scenarios based on reported ePROM interventions. Click on the links to access the publications.

An artificial standard error will be applied to this value, as specified in the Simulation tab.
